cards.q: What is an enthalpy change, \(\Delta H\)?
cards.a: The heat energy change measured under conditions of constant pressure.
cards.why: Enthalpy changes are usually given in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

cards.q: What is the sign of \(\Delta H\) for an exothermic and for an endothermic reaction?
cards.a:
Exothermic: \(\Delta H\) negative (heat given out to the surroundings).
Endothermic: \(\Delta H\) positive (heat taken in from the surroundings).
cards.why: \(\Delta H\) is measured from the point of view of the reacting chemicals: if they lose energy, \(\Delta H\) is negative.

cards.q: What are standard conditions for enthalpy changes?
cards.a: A pressure of 100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K, written \(\Delta H^{\circ}_{298}\). Each substance is in its standard state.
cards.why: The standard state is the normal physical state of the substance under these conditions, for example water as a liquid.

cards.q: Describe the enthalpy level diagram for an exothermic reaction.
cards.a: The products are drawn at a lower enthalpy level than the reactants. A downward arrow from reactants to products is labelled with the negative \(\Delta H\).
cards.why: For an endothermic reaction the products are higher than the reactants and the arrow points up.

cards.q: How does an enthalpy level diagram differ from a reaction profile diagram?
cards.a: An enthalpy level diagram shows only the levels of the reactants and products and the enthalpy change. A reaction profile also shows the energy barrier: the activation energy.
cards.why: Activation energy is not shown on an enthalpy level diagram.

cards.q: Define standard enthalpy of combustion, \(\Delta_{\text{c}}H^{\circ}\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen under standard conditions, with all reactants and products in their standard states.
cards.why: “Completely” means the products are \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\) for a hydrocarbon, not carbon monoxide or soot.

cards.q: Define standard enthalpy of formation, \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ}\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states, under standard conditions.
cards.why: By this definition, \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ}\) of an element in its standard state is zero.

cards.q: Define standard enthalpy change of reaction, \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H^{\circ}\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when the molar quantities of reactants shown in the equation react together under standard conditions, with all substances in their standard states.
cards.why: So the value depends on the equation written: doubling the equation doubles \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H^{\circ}\).

cards.q: Define standard enthalpy change of neutralisation, \(\Delta_{\text{neut}}H^{\circ}\).
cards.a: The enthalpy change when an acid and an alkali react together to form one mole of water under standard conditions.
cards.why: Defining it per mole of water lets acids with different numbers of H⁺ ions, such as HCl and H₂SO₄, be compared fairly.

cards.q: Write the equation for the standard enthalpy of formation of ethanol, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}\).
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2C(s) + 3H_{2}(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}O_{2}(g) \rightarrow C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}\)
cards.why: Exactly one mole of product, so a fraction may be needed in front of an element. Carbon is graphite in its standard state.

cards.q: Write the equation for the standard enthalpy of combustion of methane.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g) + 2O_{2}(g) \rightarrow CO_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(l)}\)
cards.why: Water is a liquid in its standard state (298 K, 100 kPa).

cards.q: Write the equation for the standard enthalpy of formation of sodium chloride.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Na(s) + \tfrac{1}{2}Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow NaCl(s)}\)
cards.why: Chlorine exists as diatomic molecules in its standard state, so half a mole is needed for one mole of NaCl.

cards.q: Why is \(\Delta_{\text{c}}H^{\circ}\) of hydrogen the same as \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ}\) of water?
cards.a: Both describe the same reaction: \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}O_{2}(g) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\).
cards.why: Burning one mole of hydrogen forms one mole of water from its elements in their standard states.

cards.q: True or false: \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ}\) of oxygen atoms, \(\mathrm{O(g)}\), is zero because oxygen is an element.
cards.a: False. Only \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\), the standard state, has \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ} = 0\).
cards.why: Making \(\mathrm{O(g)}\) from \(\mathrm{O_{2}(g)}\) needs energy to break the O=O bond, so its value is positive.

cards.q: Give the equation for the heat energy transferred in a calorimetry experiment, with units.
cards.a:
\(q = mc\Delta T\)
\(q\) in J, \(m\) in g, \(c\) in \(\text{J g}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\), \(\Delta T\) in K.
cards.why: \(m\) is the mass of the substance being heated (usually the water or solution), not the mass of the reactants. Edexcel writes \(Q\) for \(q\).

cards.q: A temperature rises from \(19.5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to \(26.0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). What is \(\Delta T\) in kelvin?
cards.why: A change of \(1\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) is the same size as a change of \(1\ \text{K}\), so a temperature difference has the same value in both.

cards.q: \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) HCl is mixed with \(25.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) NaOH in a polystyrene cup. The temperature rises by \(6.7\ \text{K}\). Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralisation. (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(-56\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
steps: Mass of solution \(= 50.0\ \text{g}\) (taking the density as \(1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}\)).
cards.why: The temperature rose, so the reaction is exothermic and the sign is negative.

cards.q: Burning \(0.460\ \text{g}\) of ethanol (\(M_{\text{r}} = 46.0\)) in a spirit burner heats \(100\ \text{g}\) of water in a copper can by \(15.0\ \text{K}\). Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{c}}H\) of ethanol. (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(-627\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: The data-book value is about \(-1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): much of the heat is lost to the surroundings.

cards.q: Explain why the enthalpy of combustion of an alcohol measured with a spirit burner and a calorimeter is much less exothermic than the data-book value.
cards.a: Heat is lost, combustion is incomplete, and conditions are not standard.
marks: Heat is lost to the surroundings and used to heat the calorimeter instead of the water.
Incomplete combustion: some carbon forms soot or carbon monoxide, releasing less energy.
Some alcohol evaporates from the wick, so the mass burned is overestimated.
The water formed is not all liquid, and conditions are not standard.

cards.q: Outline how to measure the enthalpy change of a reaction in solution, such as zinc with copper(II) sulfate solution.
cards.a: Measure the temperature before and after mixing in an insulated cup, and correct for cooling with a graph.
marks: Measure a known volume of solution into a polystyrene cup with a lid, standing in a beaker for stability.
Record the temperature every 30 s for a few minutes to get a steady starting value.
Add the second reactant (excess zinc powder) at a recorded time and stir.
Keep recording the temperature every 30 s for several minutes after the maximum.
Plot temperature against time and extrapolate the cooling line back to the time of mixing to find the corrected temperature change.

cards.q: Why is the temperature change in a calorimetry experiment found by extrapolating a graph, rather than read directly from the highest temperature recorded?
cards.a: The solution loses heat while the reaction is still happening, so the highest reading is lower than the true temperature reached.
cards.why: Extrapolating the cooling line back to the time of mixing estimates the temperature if the reaction had been instant with no heat loss.

cards.q: Excess zinc is added to \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)}\). The extrapolated temperature rise is \(10.2\ \text{K}\). Calculate \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{Zn(s) + CuSO_{4}(aq) \rightarrow ZnSO_{4}(aq) + Cu(s)}\). (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(-213\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Use the moles of the reactant that is not in excess. Zinc is in excess, so copper(II) sulfate decides how much reaction happens.

cards.q: Dissolving \(5.00\ \text{g}\) of KCl (\(M_{\text{r}} = 74.6\)) in \(50.0\ \text{g}\) of water lowers the temperature by \(5.5\ \text{K}\). Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of KCl. (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(+17\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: The temperature fell, so the process is endothermic and the sign is positive.

cards.q: \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(2.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) HCl is mixed with \(50.0\ \text{cm}^{3}\) of \(2.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\) NaOH. \(\Delta_{\text{neut}}H = -57.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the expected temperature rise. (\(c = 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}\))
cards.a: \(13.7\ \text{K}\)
cards.why: The total volume is \(100\ \text{cm}^{3}\), so the mass heated is \(100\ \text{g}\).

cards.q: What assumptions are made when calculating an enthalpy change from a reaction in solution in a polystyrene cup?
cards.a: The solution has a density of \(1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}\) and the same specific heat capacity as water; all the heat goes into the solution; the cup absorbs negligible heat.
cards.why: Each assumption makes the calculated value slightly different from the true one.

cards.q: To how many significant figures should an enthalpy change calculated from calorimetry data be given?
cards.a: To the same number of significant figures as the least precise measurement used.
cards.why: A temperature change of \(6.7\ \text{K}\) (2 s.f.) limits the answer to 2 s.f., however precise the volumes are.

cards.q: True or false: the temperature of the solution rose, so \(\Delta H\) is positive.
cards.a: False. A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic, so \(\Delta H\) is negative.
cards.why: The heat that warms the solution has been released by the reacting chemicals, which have lost energy.

cards.q: True or false: in \(q = mc\Delta T\), \(m\) is the mass of solid that dissolved or reacted.
cards.a: False. \(m\) is the mass of the substance whose temperature changes, usually the water or solution.
cards.why: Also convert \(q\) from J to kJ before dividing by moles, to give \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

cards.q: State Hess’s law.
cards.a: The enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken, provided the initial and final conditions are the same.
cards.why: It follows from conservation of energy, and lets us calculate enthalpy changes that cannot be measured directly.

cards.q: Why can \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H^{\circ}\) of methane not be measured directly, and how is it found?
cards.a: Carbon and hydrogen do not react together cleanly to form only methane. It is found with Hess’s law from the enthalpies of combustion of carbon, hydrogen and methane.
cards.why: Combustion reactions are easy to measure, so they provide the data for the cycle.

cards.q: How is \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H\) calculated from enthalpies of formation?
cards.a: \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H = \sum \Delta_{\text{f}}H( \text{products}) - \sum \Delta_{\text{f}}H( \text{reactants})\)
cards.why: The cycle goes from the elements up to the reactants and to the products. Multiply each value by the number of moles in the equation.

cards.q: How is \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H\) calculated from enthalpies of combustion?
cards.a: \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H = \sum \Delta_{\text{c}}H( \text{reactants}) - \sum \Delta_{\text{c}}H( \text{products})\)
cards.why: The cycle goes from reactants and products down to the same combustion products, so the subtraction is the other way round from formation data.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H\) for \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g) + 2O_{2}(g) \rightarrow CO_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(l)}\). \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g)}\) \(-75\), \(\mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}\) \(-394\), \(\mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}\) \(-286\).
cards.a: \(-891\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Elements in their standard states have an enthalpy of formation of zero.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{r}}H\) for \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}(s) + 3CO(g) \rightarrow 2Fe(s) + 3CO_{2}(g)}\), the main reaction in a blast furnace. \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}\) \(-824\), \(\mathrm{CO}\) \(-111\), \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\) \(-394\).
cards.a: \(-25\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Iron is an element in its standard state, so its enthalpy of formation is zero.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta_{\text{f}}H\) of ethanol from enthalpies of combustion in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): \(\mathrm{C(s)}\) \(-394\), \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g)}\) \(-286\), \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH(l)}\) \(-1367\).
cards.a: \(-279\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Oxygen is not burned, so it has no enthalpy of combustion.

cards.a: \(-137\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: With combustion data it is reactants minus products.

cards.q:
Find \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{2NaHCO_{3}(s) \rightarrow Na_{2}CO_{3}(s) + CO_{2}(g) + H_{2}O(l)}\), given:
\(\mathrm{NaHCO_{3}(s) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + CO_{2}(g) + H_{2}O(l)}\), \(\Delta H_{1} = +31\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow 2NaCl(aq) + CO_{2}(g) + H_{2}O(l)}\), \(\Delta H_{2} = -29\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.a: \(+91\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
steps: Both reactions with acid end at the same products: \(\mathrm{2NaCl(aq) + 2CO_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(l)}\).
Route 2: decomposition, then \(\mathrm{Na_{2}CO_{3}}\) with acid: \(\Delta H + \Delta H_{2}\).
cards.why: The decomposition cannot be measured directly, but both reactions with acid can be measured by calorimetry.

cards.q: Outline how to find the enthalpy change for the thermal decomposition of a hydrogencarbonate, which cannot be measured directly.
cards.a: Measure the enthalpy changes of the hydrogencarbonate and of the carbonate with acid, then combine them with Hess’s law.
marks: Add a weighed mass of the hydrogencarbonate to excess dilute hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup; record the temperature change.
Repeat with a weighed mass of the carbonate.
Calculate \(\Delta H\) in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) for each reaction using \(q = mc\Delta T\) and the moles of solid.
Construct a Hess cycle in which both reactions with acid give the same products, and combine the two values.

cards.q: The enthalpy changes of solution of anhydrous \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(s)}\) and of \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O(s)}\) are \(-66\) and \(+11\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(s) + 5H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow CuSO_{4}{\cdot}5H_{2}O(s)}\).
cards.a: \(-77\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
steps: Both solids dissolve to give the same solution, \(\mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)}\).
Direct route: \(-66\). Indirect route: hydration (\(\Delta H\)), then dissolving the hydrate (\(+11\)).
cards.why: The hydration of the anhydrous solid cannot be measured directly: it is too slow and hard to control.

cards.q: What is meant by bond enthalpy (bond dissociation enthalpy)?
cards.a: The enthalpy change needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, with all species in the gaseous state.
cards.why: For example, \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2H(g)}\) needs \(+436\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Bond breaking always needs energy.

cards.q: Define mean bond enthalpy.
cards.a: The enthalpy needed to break one mole of a given type of covalent bond in the gaseous state, averaged over a range of different compounds.
cards.why: The strength of a bond, such as C–H, varies slightly depending on the rest of the molecule, so an average is used.

cards.q: Why is breaking bonds endothermic and making bonds exothermic?
cards.a: Energy must be supplied to overcome the attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons. The same amount is released when that attraction forms.
cards.why: A reaction is exothermic overall when more energy is released making bonds than is taken in breaking them.

cards.q: How is an enthalpy change of reaction calculated from mean bond enthalpies?
cards.a: \(\Delta H = \sum( \text{bonds broken}) - \sum( \text{bonds made})\)
cards.why: Bonds broken in the reactants (taken in) minus bonds made in the products (given out). It applies to reactions where everything is gaseous.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g) + 2O_{2}(g) \rightarrow CO_{2}(g) + 2H_{2}O(g)}\). Mean bond enthalpies in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 463.
cards.a: \(-814\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Less exothermic than \(\Delta_{\text{c}}H^{\circ} = -891\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): here the water is a gas, and mean values are used.

cards.q: Calculate \(\Delta H\) for \(\mathrm{N_{2}(g) + 3H_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NH_{3}(g)}\). Bond enthalpies in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\): N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391.
cards.a: \(-93\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Count the bonds in every molecule: two ammonia molecules contain six N–H bonds.

cards.q: Explain why an enthalpy change calculated from mean bond enthalpies differs from the value found using Hess’s law with enthalpies of formation or combustion.
cards.a: Mean bond enthalpies are averages, and they apply only to gases.
marks: Mean bond enthalpies are averaged over many compounds, so they are not exact for the bonds in this particular molecule.
They apply only to the gaseous state; if a reactant or product is a liquid or solid, the energy of changing state is not included.
Enthalpies of formation or combustion are measured for the actual substances, so the Hess’s law value is more accurate.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{H_{2}(g) + Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2HCl(g)}\), \(\Delta H = -184\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Bond enthalpies: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243 \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the H–Cl bond enthalpy.
cards.a: \(+432\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
cards.why: Two H–Cl bonds are made, so divide by two.

cards.q: For \(\mathrm{CH_{4}(g) \rightarrow C(g) + 4H(g)}\), \(\Delta H = +1664\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\). Calculate the mean bond enthalpy of the C–H bond.
cards.a: \(+416\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
steps: All four C–H bonds are broken in this change.
cards.why: The four bonds are broken one after another and each needs a different amount of energy, so the value is a mean.

cards.q: Why does \(\Delta_{\text{c}}H\) become more negative by a nearly constant amount for each extra \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\) in a homologous series of alcohols?
cards.a: Each extra CH₂ adds the same extra bonds to break (one C–C, two C–H, and the O=O bonds in 1.5 more O₂) and the same extra bonds to make (in one more CO₂ and one more H₂O).
cards.why: So each step adds roughly the same energy, about \(-650\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\), and a graph of \(\Delta_{\text{c}}H\) against number of carbon atoms is a straight line.

cards.q: True or false: \(\Delta H = \sum( \text{bonds made}) - \sum( \text{bonds broken})\).
cards.a: False. \(\Delta H = \sum( \text{bonds broken}) - \sum( \text{bonds made})\).
cards.why: Breaking bonds takes energy in (positive); making bonds gives energy out (negative). Reversing the subtraction gives the wrong sign.

cards.q: Why is \(\Delta_{\text{neut}}H\) almost the same (about \(-57\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)) for any strong acid with any strong alkali?
cards.a: The reaction is always the same: \(\mathrm{H^{+}(aq) + OH^{-}(aq) \rightarrow H_{2}O(l)}\).
cards.why: Strong acids and alkalis are fully ionised, and the other ions are spectators that do not react.
